title: Yes, No, Please and Thank You
description: The small words that make you polite before you can make a sentence: yes, no, please, thanks and its reply, sorry, and the God-phrases that punctuate every Gulf conversation whatever the speaker's religiosity.
approach: GPA Phase 1 — receptive first, with short acted exchanges at a shop counter. Each particle is heard in a two-line scene before its card appears. Optional shadowing of the four replies.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 correct on the scene quiz (hear the exchange, tap the missing word)
can_do: Say yes, no, please and thank you and answer thanks
Apologise and get someone's attention politely
Use the everyday religious phrases everyone uses

culture.title: God-phrases are grammar, not piety
culture.note: إن شاء الله, الحمد لله and ما شاء الله are used by everyone in the Gulf — religious or not, Muslim or not. إن شاء الله goes in front of anything in the future ('see you tomorrow, God willing'); leaving it out sounds oddly overconfident. الحمد لله answers 'how are you' and follows every meal and piece of good news. ما شاء الله must accompany any compliment on a child, a house or a car — praising without it can make the owner uneasy. Use all three freely; nobody will read it as a religious statement.

phrases.english: God willing (any future, and a soft 'yes')
thank God (I'm fine / that went well)

culture.title: Thanks and the thanks-back
culture.note: Thanks in the Gulf is rarely a single word. Say مشكور (or شكراً) and expect a reply — العفو, or the blessing الله يسلمك. When someone hands you food or coffee, the thanks is a blessing on their hands: تسلم إيدك. When someone has worked for you (a driver, a cashier), it is يعطيك العافية, answered with الله يعافيك. Learn to hear the reply, because it tells you the exchange is closed.

phrases.english: thanks for your effort (to someone working)

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf yes is a long, relaxed ee — not the MSA نعم, which sounds like a form being filled in. Kuwait and Saudi stretch it to إيه, the Emirates and Bahrain say هيه, Jeddah says أيوه. All are accepted; إي is understood everywhere.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man nodding once with a small smile, hand raised palm-out in agreement.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any yes-no exchange; often إي والله when agreeing warmly.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Short and flat. Often doubled for emphasis (لا لا). A bare لا can sound abrupt, so it is usually softened: لا، مشكور. It is also the word that turns a command into a prohibition later on (لا تروح — don't go).
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman shaking her head gently with a polite raised palm, declining a plate.

example.english: No thanks, I don't want tea

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone declining food or an offer; the polite لا مشكور.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The all-purpose please, put before or after a request: ماي لو سمحت. To a woman it is لو سمحتي; to a group لو سمحتوا. The MSA من فضلك is understood but marks you as a textbook — nobody says it. In Saudi you will also hear الله يخليك as a warmer please.
vocabulary.image_scene: A customer at a juice stall counter, one finger raised politely toward the vendor.
vocabulary.video_hint: Ordering at a counter or asking a passer-by; the first words of most requests.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf thanks — literally 'thanked'. A woman says مشكورة, a group is told مشكورين. شكراً is also fine and universal. Hearing مشكور tells you a speaker is from the Gulf as surely as a passport.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man receiving a small coffee cup with his right hand, other hand on his chest in thanks.
vocabulary.video_hint: Receiving something across a counter; the end of an exchange.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The neutral answer to مشكور. Equally common is the blessing الله يسلمك (God keep you), which also answers goodbye — one reply, two jobs. Do not say عفواً as an apology; in the Gulf that is آسف.
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopkeeper waving off thanks with an open hand and a nod, smiling.
vocabulary.video_hint: The vendor's or host's line right after being thanked.

vocabulary.teaching_note: A woman says آسفة aasfa. Young speakers often just say سوري. In the Emirates you will hear السموحة for a light apology. The trap: معليش is 'never mind' — the reply to sorry, not sorry itself.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with a hand on his chest and an apologetic tilt of the head after bumping someone.
vocabulary.video_hint: Small collisions or late arrivals in sketches; the apology is quick and often doubled.

vocabulary.english: excuse me (to get attention / to pass)
vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'allow me' — used to catch a waiter's eye, squeeze past someone, or interrupt. لو سمحت does the same job and many people use it for both. To a woman: سمحيلي. Add يا أخوي (brother) or يا أختي (sister) to soften it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man politely edging past seated people in a crowded majlis, hand raised in apology.

example.english: Excuse me, brother — where is the door?

vocabulary.video_hint: Getting a stranger's attention in a mall or souq; squeezing through a crowd.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The word that keeps a conversation moving: 'OK', 'right then', 'fine'. Also means 'good, kind' about a person. تمام and the borrowed أوكي do the same job; ماشي too. Begins with the emphatic ط — a heavy t with a dark a after it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man giving a relaxed OK gesture with thumb and finger, nodding.
vocabulary.video_hint: Turn-taking in dialogue; the filler before a decision or a goodbye.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The warm yes: 'sure, absolutely'. طبعاً means the same. Saudis often answer a request with أبشر (consider it done), which you will hear constantly but should not try to imitate yet.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man giving an emphatic single nod and open palm, as if saying 'absolutely'.
vocabulary.video_hint: Enthusiastic agreement in sketches and vlogs; the reply to a favour asked.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Goes before any statement about the future and doubles as a soft yes or a polite maybe. Said fast as one word: inshallah. Written online as إنشالله or انشالله as often as the three-word form.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two men agreeing on a plan, one pointing upward briefly with a smile.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any mention of plans; the automatic tag on 'see you' and 'tomorrow'.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Answers 'how are you', follows a meal, greets good news and closes a story. Said as one word with the stress on the last syllable. You already met it inside بخير الحمد لله — now it stands alone.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man leaning back from an empty plate, hand on chest, content.
vocabulary.video_hint: Reply to how-are-you; after eating; at the end of a story that went well.

vocabulary.english: no problem / don't worry about it
vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'let it not concern you'. The kind reply to an apology or to a favour asked, and the phrase that dissolves awkwardness. To a woman: ولا يهمج / ولا يهمك. Gulf speakers also brush things off with عادي (it's nothing) or بسيطة (easy).
vocabulary.image_scene: A shopkeeper waving away a customer's apology with a smile and an open hand.
vocabulary.video_hint: The reply to an apology in sketches; the answer when someone asks for a favour.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Said when admiring something or someone — a child, a house, a car, a plate of food. It protects what is praised from envy, so leaving it out of a compliment can unsettle the owner. Say it and you will be forgiven every other mistake.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman admiring a baby in a stroller, hands together, delighted expression.

example.english: How lovely — the house is big

vocabulary.video_hint: House tours, babies, new cars; the automatic reaction to anything admired.

vocabulary.english: come on / let's go / OK then
vocabulary.teaching_note: Literally 'O God' but functionally 'let's go', 'hurry up', 'right then' — and, at the door, 'bye'. Written يالله or يلا. It opened Lesson 1 (tap يلّا) and it opens most Gulf goodbyes.
vocabulary.image_scene: A father at the door with car keys, beckoning children with a quick hand wave.

example.english: Come on, the car is outside

vocabulary.video_hint: Leaving the house, starting a challenge, closing a video.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.english: No, thanks. Sorry — where is the door?

dialogue.speaker: Vendor
dialogue.english: No problem — this is the door

sound_spotlight.explanation: An emphatic t: the tongue is flat and heavy and the following a sounds dark, almost like 'aw'. Compare it with the light t in تمر. Emphatics are heard here and practised in Lesson 8.
A squeezed sound from deep in the throat, written ʿ. It has no English equivalent; the trick is to hear that the vowel around it is coloured and slightly strangled. It will return in عندي and عشر.
The little catch in the throat (ʾ) at the start of a word is often dropped in Gulf speech, so آسف begins on a long, open aa. Hearing where a word really starts is half of understanding fast speech.

lesson_sequence.detail: A juice stall counter at dusk. One line of English: today you learn the words that make you polite before you can make a sentence. Tap يلّا.
Seven two-line exchanges acted at the counter (please/thanks/reply, sorry/no problem, yes, no, excuse me). Audio auto-plays; Arabic on screen; English small and grey.
Fourteen word cards with illustration and native audio, grouped: replies, particles, God-phrases. Tap to replay.
A scene replays with one line silenced; four cards appear; tap the word that belongs there. Distractors are from this lesson.
Three short authentic clips; the learner taps every time they hear إن شاء الله, الحمد لله or ما شاء الله. Counts shown afterwards.
The four replies — العفو, ولا يهمك, الحمد لله, إن شاء الله — played and echoed with a record-and-compare bar. No score.
Twelve gap-fill items, audio only. Counter rolls to 39 words. Nudge: thank someone in Arabic today and wait for the reply.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Buy one thing today and say مشكور as you take it. Listen for what comes back — العفو or الله يسلمك.
real_world_prompts.context: Lesson-complete screen. Activates the thanks pair in a guaranteed-success setting.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Every time you plan something in the next two days, add إن شاء الله in your head. Notice how often the chance comes up.
real_world_prompts.context: Next-day notification. Builds the reflex before the learner can make future sentences.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Ask your tutor to make you five offers you must decline politely: لا، مشكور. Then five you accept: إي، لو سمحت.
real_world_prompts.context: Before a tutor session. The yes/no pair with their softeners in a controlled loop.

queries: إن شاء الله الحمد لله مقطع كوميدي
video_needs.scene: Short exchanges at a shop counter or table: an order with لو سمحت, thanks and its reply, an apology and its brush-off, an إي or لا with the softener. Customer-service sketches and market vlogs are ideal.
